extracted.intended_audience: military attorneys, Army administrators, government legal officers, and adjudicators dealing with military benefits/awards/insanity/discharge issues
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/rule interpretations and administrative standards governing military matters such as insanity admissions, misconduct disqualifying gratuities, medals/certificates/badges entitlement and replacement, and related procedural requirements under statutes and War Department practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insane self-killing not suicide under policy
rubrics_metrics.description: "A self-killing by an insane person who understands the physical nature and consequences of the act, but not the moral aspect, is not a death by suicide within the meaning of a condition that a policy of insurance upon his life shall be void in case he shall die by suicide."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court authorities cited (Manhattan Life Ins. Co. v. Broughton and others) support that lack of moral understanding by the decedent negates characterization as suicide for insurance-policy forfeiture purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct disqualifying gratuity (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the gratuity statute (act of May 11, 1908, as amended), certain acts constitute 'misconduct' so as to bar payment of a gratuity to the beneficiary of a deceased officer or soldier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed examples of misconduct include: excessive use of alcohol; drinking wood alcohol; drinking bay rum and hair tonic; disobeying sentinel's order to halt; absence without leave; trespassing on railroad track; attempting to board a moving train while on furlough; presence in a house of prostitution for improper purpose; quarreling with a mistress introduced as wife; being aggressor in a fight; quarreling with a policeman; escaping while a garrison prisoner; drunkenness; quarreling in a saloon; standing up in a rowboat causing it to capsize; unauthorized sailing in bad weather likely to capsize the boat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and limits for issuing rations and reimbursements
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuing rations to destitute citizens is governed by Army Regulations; issues to entire communities (e.g., fire/flood victims) can only be authorized by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In an emergency the President has discretion to make such issues but should report action to Congress for approval. Funds appropriated by Congress for relief cannot be used to reimburse private parties for similar disbursements; a similar rule applies to reimbursements for transportation (authoritative citations provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War discretion for admission under §4843 R.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4843, R.S., authorizes admission of certain persons to the Government Hospital for the Insane on the order of the Secretary of War, but the statute is not mandatory upon the Secretary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the Secretary has discretion whether to issue the order, the superintendent of the Government Hospital must receive the patient when a proper order is made (C.19208, July 25, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insanity predating enlistment does not preclude hospital admission while enlistment stands
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier is found insane and the insanity antedated enlistment (making enlistment voidable), so long as the enlistment has not been voided the man remains a soldier and may be sent to the Government Hospital for the Insane under §4843 R.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admission may proceed under the statutory authority despite the underlying voidability of the enlistment (C.19208, Feb. 15, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to send insane prisoners to Government Hospital
rubrics_metrics.description: An insane general prisoner is usually sent to the Government Hospital for the Insane under the fifth clause of §4843 R.S.; if that clause is inapplicable, the act of June 23, 1874 may provide authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of which statutory provision applies depends on the facts of how and when insanity arose and on statutory construction (C.18802, Nov. 18, 1905).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportation incident to admission is authorized
rubrics_metrics.description: Where admission to the Government Hospital for the Insane is provided by law, transportation of the patient to the hospital is also authorized as an incident to the admission right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transportation costs are an incident of executing an admission under §4843 (C.11067, Apr. 25, 1907).

rubrics_metrics.name: Turning over insane civilian employees to local authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an insane civilian Army employee may properly be admitted to the Government Hospital under the order of the Secretary of War but declines to enter, he may be turned over to local authorities for custody and treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is applicable to civilian employees eligible under the statute who refuse admission to the Government Hospital (C.11067, Apr. 8, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of persons covered by §4843 R.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4843 R.S. (as amended) authorizes admission to the Government Hospital for the Insane of insane persons belonging to the Army and of certain insane civilian employees in the Quartermaster's, Pay, and Subsistence Departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civilians employed in other Army departments are not covered by the Secretary's authority under §4843 to send them to that hospital; the statute's coverage is limited to the named classes (C.11067, multiple dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-condition test for indigent admission (service-produced insanity)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an indigent person to be admitted under the clause relating to indigent insanity arising within three years after discharge, the insanity must both have arisen during service and have been produced by such service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insanity due to personal misconduct (not produced by service) does not satisfy the clause for admission (C.25122, June 15, 1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medal of Honor — statutory eligibility (who may receive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Medal of Honor is conferred by Congress upon officers or enlisted men 'as have most distinguished themselves in action' under the governing statutes (acts of 1862/1863 and later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute limits recipients to officers and enlisted men (not contract or acting assistant surgeons in cases where statute restricts to certain classes); analysis of whether a person qualifies depends on statutory definitions and records (citations: acts of March 3, 1863; April 23, 1904; cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medal of Honor — award must be based on official War Department records
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act of April 23, 1904, award of the Medal of Honor must appear from 'official records' in the War Department; an oral recommendation is not an official record and cannot form the basis of an award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 1904 act removes the time element in making a recommendation but requires documentary 'official records'; absence of such records is fatal to extra-statutory claims. Establishing extra-statutory time limits in executive regulation is inadvisable (G.17810; G.16305; G.19139).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medal of Honor — replacement, ownership, and wearing
rubrics_metrics.description: A Medal of Honor, once conferred, becomes the personal property (chattel) of the grantee, but it may be worn and used as a Medal of Honor only by the person upon whom it was originally conferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The act of April 23, 1904 authorizes the Secretary of War to replace lost/destroyed medals; replacement implies loss, destruction, or surrender of the old medal. The President has no authority under that act to refuse replacement when presented by the owner (G.16913; C.11582; C.16954).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medal of Honor — awards for deceased persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory scheme indicates congressional intent that the medal involve manual, personal presentation; consequently, the application for award in the case of a deceased person cannot be approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If award approval occurred before the grantee's death, the medal may be given to heirs; otherwise medals should not be granted posthumously under this interpretation (G.17605; P.49, 55; P.52, 30).

rubrics_metrics.name: Life-saving medals — jurisdictional scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Life-saving medals bestowed under the Secretary of the Treasury's authority may be given for rescues in waters 'over which the United States has jurisdiction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations of whether a particular body of water (e.g., the Quingua River in the Philippines) is within U.S. jurisdiction have been held to permit awarding life-saving medals for rescues there (G.27240, Nov. 28, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: No authority for special medals absent law/regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no authority of law for the preparation and presentation of special medals for distinguished service incident to certain operations (example: rescue of prisoners during the Philippine insurrection) unless authorized by statute or regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special medals not authorized by law/regulations are not lawful (G.12938, July 31, 1902).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized medals may not be worn on duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Medals not authorized by law or regulation cannot be worn while on duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions hold that unauthorized medals are improper uniform articles (C.5153, Oct. 18, 1898).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of Merit — eligibility and recommendation source
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the certificate-of-merit statutes (including act of Feb. 9, 1891 and amendments), an enlisted man who distinguishes himself in service may receive a certificate of merit; when belonging to a regiment, the regimental commander's recommendation is necessary (or the chief of the corps to which he belongs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The certificate is not limited to battle service and may be based on various authentic information; the recommendation may be founded on company commander recommendations or other officer reports (C.1124; C.10679; C.13084; multiple citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of Merit — timing, retired/discharged status, and pay consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A certificate of merit may be granted retrospectively in certain cases. A certificate may be given to an honorably discharged soldier with pay from the date of the gallant conduct to date of discharge only if the recommendation was made before discharge; if the recommendation is made post-discharge, the certificate generally cannot be granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A retired enlisted man is an 'enlisted man of the Army' for eligibility purposes; certificate-of-merit pay is part of soldier's pay and may be payable retroactively only when the recommendation timing and statutory requirements are met (II G; II E; C.12558; C.16315; C.23262).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of Merit — eyewitness requirement in regulations invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulatory requirement that a recommendation 'must originate with an eyewitness' is an interpolation not authorized by the statute governing certificates of merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a regulatory eyewitness-origin requirement is an instance of quasi-legislation unwarranted in Army regulations (II F; P.147, 152, May 1891).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate-of-merit pay subject to forfeiture
rubrics_metrics.description: Certificate-of-merit pay is part of a soldier's pay and is subject to forfeiture by sentence of court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards of certificate-of-merit pay may be forfeited by court-martial as they are part of pay entitlements (II K; C.1308).

rubrics_metrics.name: Badges — 'in their own right' and unauthorized society badges
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'in their own right' (regarding wearing certain society badges) means either by reason of the person's own service or by kinship to one who served; badges of certain societies (e.g., Society of Foreign Wars; Association of Military Surgeons) have no legal authority to be worn in uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions distinguish legitimate badge wearing (by statutory authorization or kinship) from unauthorized society badges which may not be worn (C.14956; C.15610).

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaign badges — entitlement and issuance rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer or enlisted man who served in a campaign recognized by a campaign badge (or who was in the service at the date when service was designated for recognition, or who is now in the service) is entitled to the badge, subject to other conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The President prescribes the manner of indicating such service (service stripes or metallic devices) and may have them procured and issued by Quartermaster's Department; several decisions clarify eligibility across regulars, volunteers, Philippine Scouts, unassigned recruits and related command structures (C.17243; II H 1; II H 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform and badge procurement/issuance limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The President prescribes uniforms and may cause devices/badges to be procured by the Quartermaster's Department and issued; however, issuing distinctive badges to volunteer officers/enlisted men no longer in service would constitute an unlawful donation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Badges may be charged to clothing allowance or issued as equipage; Quartermaster may supply badges to officers at cost; issuance to governors for organized militia use is permissible as stores and supplies under statute, but free issuance to ex-volunteers is beyond Executive power (C.23875; C.14201; C.17243; C.23839).
